title: A cache in spare memory
teaches: Caching in front of a database, hit-rate arithmetic, invalidation, and consistent hashing
summary: **A cache trades memory and data freshness for lower latency and reduced database load.** It answers repeated reads from memory so that the database processes only the misses.
**The database receives (1 − hit rate) of the reads.** Raising the hit rate from 90% to 99% cuts the database load to a tenth, making the hit rate the primary metric to monitor.

**memcached is an in-memory hash table partitioned by the client.** Servers keep no disk copies, maintain no replicas and never communicate with each other; the client hashes each key to select a server.
**With cache-aside the application coordinates the cache and the database.** It reads from the cache, queries the database on a miss, and writes the result back to the cache.

**Delete the cache entry on a write rather than updating it.** Two concurrent writers updating the cache can arrive out of order and leave a stale value in place indefinitely, whereas two deletes leave the entry empty in either order.
**A time to live bounds how stale an entry can become.** It causes misses on entries that have not changed, and acts as a fallback when invalidations fail.
**Assigning keys by hash modulo n moves almost every key when n changes.** Growing a cluster from 10 servers to 11 moves about 91% of the keys, turning the next read of each moved key into a miss.
**Consistent hashing moves only the keys that need to move.** On a ring, adding an eleventh server moves about 1/11 of the keys, which are the ones on the new server's arc.
**A database provisioned for cache misses depends on the cache.** Once the database is sized only for the miss traffic, a cache failure exposes it to the full read workload.

blocks.text: By 2003 LiveJournal's databases were busy again, now with reads. The clusters from Lesson 4 had divided the writes, but the same popular journal entries, friends lists and user records were read thousands of times a second, and each read was a query on a database. Meanwhile the web servers, dozens of them, each had memory to spare. They needed processor time to build pages, but not much RAM to hold them.

In May 2003 Brad Fitzpatrick wrote a program to put that spare memory to work. It ran on any machine with RAM to give and stored values under keys, handing them back when asked. He called it **memcached**. It kept nothing on disk, made no copies, and its servers did not know about each other. If one restarted, whatever it held was gone, and the program reading from it queried the database instead, as it would have without the cache. Within a few years Facebook, Wikipedia, YouTube, Twitter and thousands of other sites ran it.[^memcached]

A **cache** is any store that keeps copies of data from a slower source so that repeated reads can be answered with lower latency. In this lesson, we will evaluate how much load and latency a cache saves, and what it costs in return. Both come down to one number, the hit rate, defined below.

On each server memcached is a **hash table** in memory. Each item holds a key of up to 250 bytes, a value of up to 1 megabyte, an expiry time and a few flags. When memory runs out, it discards the item that has gone longest without being read; this is called evicting the **least recently used** (LRU) item, and it means the cache fills itself with whatever is read most without an administrator configuring it.[^slabs] The client communicates with the server over TCP in lines of plain text to set a key with a value and a lifetime, get a key, or delete a key.

blocks.caption: What memcached sends over the network and keeps in memory. A get command that finds nothing returns END, and the application queries the database.

blocks.text: The cluster has no leader and no shared state. The client library holds the list of servers and picks one for each key by hashing it, so the same key always goes to the same server. The latency figures from Lesson 1 show why querying a cache on another machine is worthwhile. A network round trip inside the datacentre takes about 0.5 ms, while a database query that reads from disk takes several milliseconds, and one that queues behind other queries (Lesson 2) takes even longer.

The usual way to use memcached is called **cache-aside**, where the application queries the cache first. If the item is there (a **hit**), the cache returns the answer. If not (a **miss**), the application queries the database, sends the reply on, and stores it in the cache for next time. The cache never communicates with the database; the application handles both steps.

The **hit rate**, the fraction of reads the cache answers, determines the system's performance. With a hit rate h, the database receives (1 − h) of the reads. The mean read latency is h times the cache latency plus (1 − h) times the database latency. Consider a workload of 20,000 reads a second, a database with a capacity of 4,000 reads a second, a cache read latency of 0.5 ms and a database read latency of 10 ms.

blocks.caption: Cache-aside at 20,000 reads a second in front of a database with a capacity of 4,000 reads a second (the dots run at a two-hundredth of that rate, in slow motion). Blue dots are requests and green dots are responses. A request answered at the cache is a hit, and one that proceeds to the database is a miss.
blocks.task: Estimate how much the database load falls when the hit rate rises from 90% to 99%, then raise the hit rate to 99%.

blocks.text: At a 90% hit rate the database receives 2,000 reads a second, half its capacity, and the mean read latency is 1.45 ms. At 99% the database receives 200 reads a second, and the mean latency is 0.6 ms. Increasing the hit rate from 90% to 99% looks like a small improvement, but it cuts database load tenfold because the miss rate falls from 10% to 1%. At an 80% hit rate the database receives 4,000 reads a second and reaches saturation. Small changes in a high hit rate change the database load by large factors, which is why engineers monitor the hit rate closely.

The hit rate depends on how reads are distributed across keys and how much memory the cache has. Read distributions on most sites are heavily skewed, meaning a small fraction of items receives most of the reads. If the most popular 5% of items account for 90% of the reads, a cache large enough to hold that 5% achieves a 90% hit rate, and doubling its memory may add only a few percentage points. To size a cache, you can log the keys read over a busy hour, sort them by request frequency, and sum the sizes of the most-read keys until they cover your target hit rate. That total, the **working set**, is the memory capacity the cache requires. This arithmetic also works in reverse. Once a database is provisioned only for the misses, it depends on the cache to survive. If the hit rate drops from 99% to 90% because a cache server restarts empty, the database load increases tenfold. When many reads miss at once and hit the database together, they cause a **miss storm**, which we will address in Lesson 15.

A cache holds copies, and copies become stale when the underlying data changes. Engineers use two mechanisms to bound staleness. The first is a **time to live** (TTL), where each item expires after a set duration, such as five minutes, and the next read fetches a fresh copy from the database. An entry is never more than five minutes stale, at the cost of misses on items that have not changed. The second mechanism is **invalidation**: when the application writes to the database, it also removes or updates the cache entry. When invalidation works, readers see changes immediately; when it fails, they read stale data indefinitely. Most systems combine both, using invalidation for freshness and a TTL as a fallback for failed invalidations.[^karlton] You choose the TTL based on how much staleness each type of data can tolerate: a user's display name can be an hour out of date, whereas an inventory count might tolerate only a few seconds of staleness. A TTL much shorter than the average time between reads of a key turns every read into a miss.

The simplest invalidation strategy is to update the cache with the new value on every write, but this introduces a race condition. Suppose two writers update the same row at nearly the same time: writer A writes v1 to the database, and then writer B writes v2. Each writer then sends its value to the cache. If writer A is delayed between its two steps by a runtime pause or a slow network packet, writer B's cache update arrives first and writer A's arrives second. The database now holds v2 while the cache holds v1, and the cache will serve stale data until the entry expires.

blocks.caption: Two writers update the same row, and writer A pauses briefly between updating the database and updating the cache. Time runs down the page.
blocks.task: Run the simulation with set on write, then with delete on write.

blocks.text: Deleting the entry instead of setting it prevents this race condition. Two deletes in either order leave the cache entry empty, and the next read fetches the current value from the database. The trade-off is one extra miss after every write. A narrower race condition remains, in which a reader fetches an old value from the database just before a write and writes it to the cache just after the delete. Facebook encountered this race at scale and solved it with leases, as we will see in Lesson 15.

Early memcached clients chose a server by hashing the key to an integer and taking the remainder modulo the number of servers. With 10 servers, a key whose hash is 4,417 goes to server 7. Modulo hashing distributes keys evenly and is fast to compute, but it fails when a server is added or removed. With 11 servers, 4,417 mod 11 is 6, and almost every key maps to a different server. Growing the cluster from 10 servers to 11 moves about 10 keys in 11 (91%). Each moved key causes a miss on its new server, so adding cache capacity temporarily drops the hit rate from 90% to about 8%, as only the one key in 11 that stayed in place can still hit. By our earlier arithmetic, misses rise from 10% of reads to 92%, sending the database more than nine times its normal load.

In 1997 David Karger and colleagues at MIT published a solution to this problem for web caches, which they called **consistent hashing**.[^karger] We hash both the servers and the keys onto a circle, and assign each key to the first server clockwise from its position. Adding a server places one new point on the circle, so only the keys between the new server and the previous one change hands, which is about 1/11 of the keys in an 11-server cluster. Removing a server hands its keys to the next server clockwise and leaves all other keys in place.

blocks.caption: Keys hashed onto a circle. With modulo n hashing, keys move to new servers almost entirely; on a ring, only the keys on the new server's arc change hands.
blocks.task: Add a server with modulo n hashing, then switch to the ring and add one there.

blocks.text: If each server is placed at only one point on the circle, the arcs between them will have uneven lengths, giving some servers twice their share of keys and others half. To even out the distribution, we place each server at many points around the circle so the arc lengths average out. With 100 or more points per server, the key counts on each server stay within roughly 10% of one another. We will revisit this technique in Lesson 12 with Amazon's Dynamo, which popularised it. Memcached clients adopted consistent hashing in 2007 when engineers at Last.fm released libketama, a library that placed each server at 160 points on the ring, and other client libraries soon copied the design.

We can now quantify the trade-offs of adding a cache. It reduces read latency and allows the database to be a tenth or a hundredth of the size it would otherwise need to be. In exchange, it requires memory, which is free when spare RAM is available on web servers, but adds hardware cost when provisioned on dedicated machines. It reduces data freshness, requiring you to specify how stale each type of read is allowed to be. It adds application complexity, because with cache-aside every read path must handle misses and every write path must handle invalidation. Finally, it introduces an operational dependency, because a database provisioned only for the miss traffic cannot handle the full read workload if the cache fails.

Cache-aside is not the only caching architecture. A **read-through** cache fetches data from the database itself on a miss, so the application communicates only with the cache. A **write-through** cache accepts writes and forwards them to the database, updating its own state at the same time. Both architectures move the miss and invalidation logic out of the application, and both place the cache directly on the critical path that must not fail. Memcached implemented a cache that knows nothing about the database and left the coordination to the application, which made it straightforward to adopt across different systems.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Database load = (1 − hit rate) × read rate; mean latency = h × cache latency + (1 − h) × database latency.
Delete the cache entry on write, and set a TTL as a fallback.
On a consistent-hashing ring, adding the nth server moves about 1/n of the keys, whereas modulo n hashing moves almost all of them.

blocks.caption: Seven questions on caching
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: A cache in front of a database answers 95% of 40,000 reads a second. How many reads a second reach the database?
items.why: The database receives the misses, which is (1 − 0.95) × 40,000 = 2,000 reads a second. At a 99% hit rate it would receive 400 reads a second.

items.ask: A team raises its cache hit rate from 90% to 99% by adding memory. What effect does this have on the database's read load?
choices: It reduces the load by about a tenth, since 99% is a tenth higher than 90%
It reduces the load to a tenth, since misses fall from ten in a hundred to one in a hundred
It leaves the load almost unchanged, since most reads were hits already
items.why: The database load equals the miss rate multiplied by the total read rate. Misses fall from 10% to 1%, so the database receives a tenth as many reads.

items.ask: Why should a writer delete the cache entry after updating the database, rather than setting it to the new value?
choices: Deleting is faster on the cache server than storing a new value of the same size, so writes return sooner
Two concurrent sets can arrive out of order, whereas two deletes leave the same result in either order
A set can fail when memory is full, leaving the old value cached
items.why: If writer A sets v1 after writer B sets v2, the cache retains v1 while the database holds v2. Two deletes leave the entry empty regardless of order, and the next read fetches the current value from the database.

items.ask: A memcached cluster assigns keys by hash modulo n. It grows from 20 servers to 21 during the evening peak. What happens?
choices: About one key in 21 moves, so the hit rate dips by a few percentage points
Nothing moves until each item's time to live expires, so the change is spread over several minutes
About 20 keys in 21 map to a different server, so nearly every read misses at once
items.why: With modulo n hashing, almost every key maps to a different server when n changes. Each moved key causes a miss, and the database suddenly receives nearly the full read workload. Consistent hashing moves only about 1/21 of the keys.

items.ask: On a consistent-hashing ring with ten cache servers, one server fails. Which keys change server?
choices: Only the keys that were assigned to the failed server, which move to the next server clockwise
About half of all keys, since the remaining nine servers must rebalance the load among themselves
All keys, since every key's position on the ring is recomputed from the new server count
items.why: Each key belongs to the first server clockwise from its position. Removing one server's point on the ring changes the owner only for the keys on its arc.

items.ask: A database has a capacity of 3,000 reads a second. The site serves 50,000 reads a second through a cache with a 98% hit rate. A cache server restarts and drops the hit rate to 90% for a few minutes. What happens?
choices: The database load rises from 1,000 to 5,000 reads a second, exceeding its capacity
The database load rises by about 8% and stays within its capacity
The database load does not change, because cache misses are answered by the other cache servers
items.why: At a 98% hit rate, the database receives 2% of 50,000 reads, or 1,000 reads a second. At 90%, it receives 10%, or 5,000 reads a second. A database provisioned only for the misses depends on the hit rate staying high.

items.ask: Why did memcached keep no copies on disk and no replicas?
choices: Disks and networks in 2003 were too slow to keep up with the write throughput of a cache
Every entry could be rebuilt from the database, so losing a server caused cache misses rather than data loss
Replication would have required the servers to elect a leader, which software of the time could not do
items.why: The database remains the source of truth. Losing a cache server causes a burst of misses, and omitting disk persistence and replication kept memcached simple, fast and easy to operate.

memcached.title: Perl, then C
memcached.text: The first version of memcached was written in Perl in May 2003, and Anatoly Vorobey rewrote it in C that summer for performance. Fitzpatrick's company Danga Interactive released it as free software, and its plain-text protocol made it easy for developers to write client libraries in every major programming language.

slabs.title: Slabs
slabs.text: To avoid the memory fragmentation caused by allocating and freeing values of arbitrary sizes, memcached divides its memory into 1 MB pages and slices each page into fixed-size chunks called slabs. Each slab class holds chunks slightly larger than the previous class, and memcached stores each item in the smallest chunk that fits it. Each slab class maintains its own least-recently-used eviction list.

karlton.title: Two hard things
karlton.text: An observation attributed to Phil Karlton, a programmer at Netscape, states that there are only two hard things in computer science: cache invalidation and naming things. Programmers often add off-by-one errors as a third.

karger.title: From web caches to Akamai
karger.text: Karger's group designed consistent hashing to distribute web pages across proxy caches so that a popular page would not overload any single machine. Two of the paper's co-authors, Tom Leighton and Danny Lewin, founded Akamai in 1998 using this research, building the first large content delivery network (Lesson 19).
